DOCUMENT:
Pricing Proposal: Weekend Rate Restructure
Harbourside Hotel, Revenue Management, April 2026

1. Proposal
From 1 June 2026 we propose to (a) raise the Best Available Rate (BAR) for Friday and Saturday nights from £145 to £165, and (b) introduce a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday night. Midweek rates are unchanged.

2. Context
Harbourside is a 112-room four-star hotel on the quay, with a leisure-led weekend business and a corporate-led midweek business. Our weekend BAR is £20 to £35 below the three comparable hotels in our competitive set, whose weekend rates currently range from £165 to £180. Weekend occupancy has recovered strongly since 2023 and we believe we are leaving money on the table.

Table 1. Weekend (Friday and Saturday) occupancy by month, 2025
Jan 62% | Feb 66% | Mar 74% | Apr 80% | May 85% | Jun 81%
Jul 89% | Aug 93% | Sep 88% | Oct 82% | Nov 72% | Dec 78%

Average weekend occupancy across 2025 was 79%. July and August are our strongest months, driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays, with September also benefiting from late-season visitors.

3. Evidence on price sensitivity
In the last week of June 2025 we raised the weekend BAR by £10, from £135 to the current £145. Weekend occupancy in July rose to 89%, from 81% in June. This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels; if anything, the higher rate appears to have reinforced our positioning as a quality option, and we expect the further increase to be absorbed in the same way.

This is consistent with feedback from our guest satisfaction surveys, where weekend guests rate "value for money" at 8.4 out of 10, the highest score among our competitive set.

4. Two-night minimum
Saturday nights are our most constrained inventory: we sold out on 31 Saturdays in 2025. Many of these guests stay only one night, leaving rooms empty on Friday or Sunday either side. A two-night minimum for stays including a Saturday will convert single-night Saturday stays into two-night stays and smooth occupancy across the weekend.

Our booking data show that weddings at Quayside Hall, the venue next door, account for around 38% of our Saturday-night room bookings. Wedding guests typically book as a block through the couple, arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning.

5. Revenue impact
Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%, a £20 increase in BAR is worth about £204,000 a year in additional room revenue, before any gain from longer stays. We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above.

The two-night minimum should add further revenue through additional Friday and Sunday nights. We have not quantified this but expect it to be material, particularly in shoulder months.

6. Implementation and monitoring
The new rates will be loaded into the channel manager on 15 May for stays from 1 June, giving online travel agencies two weeks' notice. Corporate contracted rates and group rates already contracted will be honoured. We will review pick-up weekly against the same weeks in 2025 and report to the General Manager monthly. If weekend occupancy for any month falls more than five points below 2025, we will review the rate.

7. Recommendation
The evidence shows that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current rates and that we are priced well below our competitive set. We recommend approval of the £165 weekend BAR and the two-night Saturday minimum from 1 June 2026, delivering at least £204,000 of additional annual room revenue.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%" -- The hotel is described as a 112-room hotel in the Context section, but the revenue estimate uses 124 rooms. With 112 rooms the same calculation gives 112 x 104 x 0.79 x £20 = about £184,000, not £204,000.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels" -- The only evidence is that occupancy rose from June to July after a June rate rise, but the document itself says July and August are the strongest months because of the harbour festival and school holidays. The seasonal rise confounds the comparison; it cannot show demand is price-insensitive (let alone that the higher price helped).
3. [missing_consideration] at: "We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above." -- The document states that about 38% of Saturday-night bookings are wedding guests from the adjacent venue who stay only Saturday night. A two-night minimum would exclude or deter this group, but the revenue case assumes occupancy is maintained and never addresses the loss of these single-night Saturday bookings.

REVIEW:
# Review: Weekend Rate Restructure Proposal

The proposal is clearly structured, the case that rates are low compared with competitors is well made, and the monitoring plan is sensible. But it has five significant problems:

- The revenue estimate uses the **wrong room count**.
- It applies the rate rise to rooms that **won't be sold at the new rate**.
- The price-sensitivity "test" is **confounded by the season**.
- The two-night minimum **conflicts with the hotel's largest Saturday segment**.
- The rate rise needs to be presented as **reaching the bottom of the competitor range**, not staying below it.

The £204,000 figure is not a floor. It's closer to an upper bound.

## 1. The hotel has 112 rooms, not 124

Section 2 describes a **112-room** hotel. The revenue calculation uses **124 rooms**:

| | Rooms | Calculation | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Paper | 124 | 124 × 104 × 79% × £20 | **£203,757** |
| Corrected | 112 | 112 × 104 × 79% × £20 | **£184,038** |

Correcting the room count alone removes about **£20,000**. The average occupancy of 79% (79.2%) and the 104 weekend nights are both correct.

## 2. The £20 doesn't apply to every room sold at weekends

The calculation assumes every occupied weekend room gains £20. But:

- **Weddings account for about 38% of Saturday-night room bookings**, typically as blocks booked through the couple. Group rates already contracted will be honoured, and future wedding blocks are likely to be negotiated separately rather than sold at BAR.
- **Corporate rates, packages and promotions** won't necessarily move with BAR.
- **Online travel agency commissions**, typically 15–20%, reduce the net gain on rooms sold through those channels.
- **Bookings already made** for June–August at £145 will be honoured. Leisure guests often book summer weekends months ahead, so the first months will see little of the increase.

A realistic estimate applies the £20 only to the **share of weekend rooms sold at BAR**, net of commission. That share could plausibly be half or less of weekend occupancy, which would put the gain nearer **£80,000–£100,000** than £204,000. The hotel's own channel and segment data would give the actual figure.

## 3. The June–July comparison doesn't test price sensitivity

The rate went up in the last week of June 2025, and occupancy rose from 81% to 89% in July. But section 2 itself says **July and August are the strongest months because of the harbour festival and the school holidays**. The rise is what the season would produce anyway, so the comparison can't separate the price effect from the seasonal one.

The month-to-month pattern actually points the other way: occupancy *fell* from 85% in May to 81% in June. A proper test would compare:
- **July 2025 against July 2024**, at the old rate, or
- months after the price rise against the same months a year earlier, for example October–December.

Neither comparison is in the paper.

**The value-for-money score of 8.4** was earned at £135–145, the lowest rates in the competitive set. It shows guests value the hotel *at current prices*. It doesn't show they'll rate it as highly at £165.

## 4. The two-night minimum may cost revenue rather than add it

The paper treats the minimum as pure upside, and the author describes it as unquantified extra value. But section 4 includes the key fact: **wedding guests, about 38% of Saturday bookings, typically stay Saturday night only.**

- If the minimum applies to wedding guests, many will **book elsewhere** rather than pay for two nights. That puts at risk both the hotel's largest Saturday segment and its relationship with Quayside Hall.
- If it **doesn't** apply to them, the main group it's meant to convert is excluded.
- The hotel sold out on **31 Saturdays**, so there were **about 21 Saturdays without a sell-out**. On those nights the minimum would turn away single-night guests the hotel could have accommodated.

The minimum makes most sense on **sell-out Saturdays only**. It's common to apply it selectively, based on demand, rather than as a blanket rule.

## 5. £165 matches the cheapest competitor

Competitors charge **£165–£180**, so £165 puts Harbourside **at the bottom of the range**, level with the cheapest competitor rather than below it. That may be the right price for a four-star hotel on the quay. But the hotel will lose the clear value advantage that probably explains part of the 8.4 score. The paper should present the change that way, rather than implying the hotel stays cheaper than its competitors.

## 6. Monitoring

The trigger, a month more than five points below 2025, is reasonable. It would help to add the **break-even point**: at £165 against £145, room revenue is maintained unless occupancy falls by more than about **12%**, from 79% to roughly 69.5%, a fall of about **9–10 points**. A five-point fall would still be revenue-positive. Stating this tells the GM what the trigger actually means.

Monitor **booking pace for Saturdays with weddings** separately as well, since that's where the two-night minimum carries the most risk.

## Author's description compared with the document

| Author's claim | What the document shows |
|---|---|
| Built on own trading history | ✓, but the one test is confounded |
| Occupancy rose after the June 2025 rise | July is peak season; the rise is seasonal |
| Value score 8.4, the best in the set | ✓, earned at the lowest rates in the set |
| Rates £20–35 below competitors | ✓ today; at £165 the hotel matches the cheapest |
| £204,000 is a floor | Uses 124 rooms (actual 112); applies £20 to all rooms including group and wedding blocks; ignores commissions |
| Two-night minimum is unvalued upside | May lose wedding business (38% of Saturdays) and single-night stays on the ~21 non-sell-out Saturdays |
| Clear monitoring trigger | ✓, but should be paired with the break-even figure |

## Recommendations

1. Correct the room count to 112.
2. Recalculate the gain using the BAR share of weekend rooms, net of OTA commission, and allow for bookings already on the books.
3. Replace the June–July evidence with year-on-year comparisons, or acknowledge that price sensitivity hasn't been tested.
4. Rethink the two-night minimum. Apply it selectively on high-demand Saturdays, and decide explicitly how wedding blocks are handled. Talk to Quayside Hall before 1 June.
5. Present £165 as matching the bottom of the competitor range, and add the break-even occupancy figure to the monitoring section.

The rate increase looks well justified: the hotel is clearly underpriced compared with its competitors, and the break-even margin is comfortable. The two-night minimum carries more risk than the paper acknowledges. With corrected figures, the GM can approve the rate rise knowing what it will actually deliver, and decide on the minimum-stay rule separately.
